title: The morning brightness
hookLine: after a painful pause in revelation, Surah Ad-Duha comes: your Lord has not forsaken you

lines: TWO OR THREE NIGHTS, AND A TAUNT.
cards: After the cave, after iqra, after Waraqa, the hadith says, the revelation paused. Nothing came, and the reports don't agree on how long.
A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari remembers another silence: two or three nights when he was unwell and did not rise to pray, and a woman who taunted him that his companion seemed to have left him.
Silence, and then mockery about the silence. The surah that answered it is today's.

teach.h: BY THE MORNING, BY THE STILL NIGHT.
teach.b: Then it comes: Surah Ad-Duha, the ninety-third.
In Pickthall's translation: “By the morning hours And by the night when it is stillest, Thy Lord hath not forsaken thee nor doth He hate thee.”
Ad-duha is the bright part of the morning, when the sun is well up and the day is fully warm. And the surah swears by two things together: the full light of morning, and the still night.
As if to say: the night was real, and quiet, and that quiet was not abandonment. The morning comes after it, as sure as the sun.
Then, gently: what comes later will be better for you than what came before, and your Lord will give you until you are content. Then it reminds him of his own life.
Did He not find you an orphan, and shelter you? Find you wandering, and guide you? Find you in need, and enrich you?
You heard the first of those on day eighty, with Halimah. You were never left before, and you aren't left now.
The surah ends by turning the comfort outward: don't be harsh with the orphan, don't turn away the one who asks, and, in Pickthall's words: “Therefor of the bounty of thy Lord be thy discourse.”

Speak of the good you've been given. Some Muslims turn to this surah in the dark stretches of their own lives: after a loss, in depression, when prayer feels like shouting into an empty room. It doesn't deny the night.
It swears by it. And then it says: morning.

how: Surah Ad-Duha is short, and some Muslims recite it in times of sadness; some also pray a voluntary prayer called duha in the bright part of the morning.

o: the evening glow as the sun goes down
the first pale light just before dawn
the bright part of the morning, sun well up

games.q: what's inside the surah — tap the pairs.
p: the bright part of the morning

s: the revelation never paused after the first night
it stopped for a time; the reports differ on how long.
Ad-Duha swears by the night as well as the morning
by the morning hours and by the night when it is stillest (93:1–2).
the surah tells him to keep his blessings to himself
it ends: of the bounty of thy Lord be thy discourse (93:11).

games.q: the revelation has gone silent, and someone in town mocks the Prophet: your companion has left you. what comes next?
o: a surah: thy Lord hath not forsaken thee.
a vision telling him to leave Mecca.
games.why: Surah Ad-Duha: by the morning hours and by the night when it is stillest, thy Lord hath not forsaken thee nor doth He hate thee.

practice: Sit in the light for a minute: a window or the open air by day, a lamp by night, or just the memory of the last morning light you felt on your face.

With your eyes closed, think of one silent stretch in your life that turned out not to be abandonment. If you pray, you can recite the opening: by the morning hours, and by the night when it is stillest.

wordCard.voice: Ad-duha, the morning brightness: the surah that came after a silence to say your Lord has not forsaken you.

orig.note: Arabic: the full brightness of morning; the name of Surah 93.

carryVoice: Your line: you have not been forsaken. Tomorrow, the first people who believed. Day eighty-nine, done.
